links.note: 221 says only giving to those who have nothing (வறியார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈவதே) is giving, and every other gift has the nature of குறியெதிர்ப்பை, a loan to be returned in the same measure. 211 says obligation wants no return (கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு) and asks what the world gives back to the rain. Read together, the rain is the model of the giver whom 221 defines by exclusion: one whose recipient cannot repay.

221 restricts ஈகை to gifts to the destitute and classes 'all the rest' (மற்றெல்லாம்) as exchange. 212 says all wealth earned by effort exists for வேளாண்மை toward the deserving (தக்கார்க்கு), with no mention of need. The conflict holds if 221's 'all the rest' is taken to cover help to the worthy who are not poor; Parimelazhagar avoids it by treating ஒப்புரவு and ஈகை as separate virtues and limiting 'the rest' to gifts made to the non-poor with a benefit in view.

221 sets true giving against gifts that carry a measured return (குறியெதிர்ப்பை). 103, in the chapter on gratitude, says help done by those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி) is larger than the sea when its goodness is weighed. The same test, absence of calculation, is applied once from the giver's side and once from the receiver's.

222 says taking is bad even if it were called a good path (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது). 1054 says that asking from those who do not know concealment even in a dream is itself like giving (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும்). They conflict if கொளல் is read, with Parimelazhagar, as accepting alms without exception; on Kalaignar's reading of கொளல் as taking goods from others by whatever fair means, the two address different acts.

222 holds receiving to be bad whatever is said in its favour. 1061 says that not asking is worth a crore even from those dear as one's eyes who give gladly without hiding (கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார் கண்ணும் இரவாமை). Both refuse the best case that could be made for receiving: 222 the claim that it is a good path, 1061 the excellence of the giver.

223 says that not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' (இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை) and giving are found only in one of good family (குலனுடையான் கண்ணே). 955 says an old family does not part from its nature even when what it can give has shrunk (வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்). The chapter on giving and the chapter on lineage make the same claim: generosity that outlasts means is the mark of birth.

On Parimelazhagar's first reading, 223 says the well-born do not speak to others the beggar's degrading word 'I am poor'. 1044 says that even in the well-born (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும்) poverty produces the lapse from which degrading words are born (இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு). The conflict depends on that reading of 223; if 'இலன்' is the giver's refusal to an asker, as Pope takes it, the two speak of different utterances.

Both verses turn on the quoted plea 'I have nothing': 223 has இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம், 205 has இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க. In 205 the plea is an excuse for doing evil and is answered with the warning that one will have nothing all over again; in 223 it is a plea the well-born do not voice. In both the book refuses to let want serve as a reason.

224 gives the giver's side: being asked is painful (இன்னாது இரக்கப்படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face (இன்முகம்). 1057 gives the asker's side: on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt, the heart rejoices deep within (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து). The two describe one moment from both ends, and the asker's gladness in 1057 is what ends the giver's discomfort in 224.

In 224 the giver watches the asker's face and is uneasy until it turns glad. In 90 the guest watches the host's face and wilts, like the anicham flower when smelled, if that face changes (முகந்திரிந்து நோக்க). The face is the measure of the exchange in both, read in opposite directions.

224 says the unease of being asked lasts until the asker's face is glad. 228 names what follows as a pleasure in its own right, ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம், which Parimelazhagar explains as the joy the giver has from the receiver's rejoicing. 228 then uses that pleasure as a charge against those who hoard and lose.

225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and that it comes after (பின்) the strength of those who remove hunger. 160 says those who fast in penance are great, but after (பின்) those who endure others' harsh words. The same construction is used twice to rank fasting below a virtue practised among other people.

225 places the ascetic's endurance of hunger behind the power of the one who relieves it. 48 says the household life that keeps others on their way without slipping from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). Both rank the householder's provision above the austerity it supports.

225 ranks relieving hunger above bearing it. 263 asks whether the others have forgotten austerity out of a wish to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி); Parimelazhagar takes 'the others' as householders. Read with 225, the verse from the austerity chapter concedes that the renouncer's fast depends on someone else's giving.

226 says that removing the ruinous hunger of the destitute (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where one who has gained wealth stores it (பெற்றான் பொருள் வைப்புழி). 333 says wealth by nature does not stay, so on gaining it (அது பெற்றால்) one should at once do what stays (அற்குப). 226 supplies the concrete act for 333's general rule.

Both verses use the act of putting wealth away (வை). In 226 feeding the destitute is the வைப்புழி, the place of deposit; in 228 the hard-eyed 'keep and lose' what they own (வைத்திழக்கும்). The chapter sets a store that holds beside a store that is lost.

227 says the evil disease called hunger hardly touches one accustomed to shared eating (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). 44 uses the same word: if a life fears blame and has பாத்தூண், its line never fails. The same practice is given a reward for the person in 227 and for the lineage in 44.

227 promises that the one who shares his food will not meet hunger. 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats what is left even needs sowing (வித்தும் இடல் வேண்டும் கொல்லோ). Both state as a rule that feeding others first secures one's own food.

227 praises habitual shared eating (பாத்தூண்). In 1107 the man compares his beloved's embrace to living in one's own home and eating one's own food after sharing it (தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று). The lover's simile takes the householder's sharing of 227 as its standard of pleasure.

228 asks whether the hard-eyed who keep what they have and lose it (வைத்திழக்கும்) do not know the joy of giving. 88 says those who do not take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods with care and end by saying 'we have no support' (பரிந்தோம்பிப் பற்றற்றேம் என்பர்); Parimelazhagar reads this as losing what was guarded. Both describe the same course: keeping, then loss.

228 speaks of a pleasure the hoarder never learns, ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம். 598, which Parimelazhagar applies to kings, says those without inner drive never reach the proud joy of saying 'we have been generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னும் செருக்கு). The pleasure of giving is missed through hardness in the one verse and through lack of energy in the other.

228 says only that the hoarder keeps his goods and loses them. 1009 says how: bright wealth gathered by giving up love, denying oneself and ignoring virtue is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The later verse fills in the 'losing' of 228.

229 says that eating alone (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) in order to fill one's store is more bitter than begging. 82 says that eating by oneself while the guest is outside is not to be wished even if the food were the medicine of deathlessness (சாவா மருந்தெனினும்). Both condemn the solitary meal, one by ranking it below begging and one by refusing it even at the highest value.

229 condemns those who eat alone to build up their own wealth. 527 says crows do not hide their food but call and eat (காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும்), and that gain belongs only to those of that nature. The rule against eating alone appears in the ethics of giving in 229 and as advice on keeping kin and prosperity in 527.

230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is not possible (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). 219 says the poverty of a person of நயன் consists in being unable to do the things he would do (செயும் நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா ஆறு). 219 defines the condition, and 230 says how the giver values it: below death.

230 holds death sweet for one who can no longer give. 968 asks whether a life of tending the flesh is any medicine once greatness has lost its dignity (பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து). In both a life is not worth keeping once the thing that gave it worth is gone: giving in 230, honour in 968.

1041 says that the only thing as painful as poverty is poverty itself (இன்மையின் இன்மையே இன்னாதது). 230 opens by saying nothing is more painful than death (சாதலின் இன்னாதது இல்லை), then reverses it for the person who cannot give. Taken together, 230's second half brings it into line with 1041: the want that stops giving is placed above death in bitterness.

231 says that apart from living with renown through giving there is no profit for a living being (அது அல்லது ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு). 122 says no gain for a living being is greater than restraint (ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு). Read literally the two exclusive claims cannot both hold; the conflict disappears if each is taken as the emphasis its own chapter gives its subject.

231 ends 'ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு' and 31 ends 'ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு': both use the figure of profit to a living being. 31 gives the place to virtue in general, which yields distinction and wealth; 231 gives it to renown that comes from giving. The shared formula shows 231 naming one particular form of the gain that 31 states broadly.

232 says that everything speakers say comes to rest as praise on those who give to those who ask (இரப்பார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈவார்மேல் நிற்கும் புகழ்). 1059 asks what standing givers would have if there were none who wished to ask and receive (இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை); Parimelazhagar takes தோற்றம் there as renown. The giver's fame in 232 therefore depends on the asker.

232 makes giving the subject of all praise. 296 says there is no renown like not lying (பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை). They conflict if both are read as naming the single greatest source of renown; Parimelazhagar's gloss on 296, that truthfulness is the cause of renown in this life, keeps the claim just as strong.

232 says the world's speech settles as praise on the giver. 387 says that for one able to give and protect with sweet words (இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்கு), this world is as his own word would have it. In the chapter on kingship the same giving that earns the world's words in 232 earns its compliance.

233 says that nothing in the world stands without perishing (பொன்றாது நிற்பது) except high renown. 36 calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). The same word marks two different survivals: renown remains in the world (உலகத்து), and virtue goes with the person who dies.

233 says only renown stands undying. 156 says those who punish have a day's pleasure, while those who forbear have renown பொன்றுந் துணையும், which Pope and Parimelazhagar take as until the world ends. 156 measures a virtue's reward by the lasting quality that 233 attributes to renown, and gives it a source other than giving.

233 says renown is the one thing that stands undying (பொன்றாது நிற்பது). 145 says the man who enters another's home thinking it easy gets blame that stands without ever dying (எஞ்ஞான்றும் விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). Blame is given the same permanence as renown, which strains 233's 'nothing else' if that phrase is read strictly.

234 says that if a person achieves far-reaching renown within the earth's bounds (நிலவரை நீள்புகழ் ஆற்றின்), the world of the gods will not honour the புலவர், whom Parimelazhagar takes to be the sages who have reached it. 50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived (வையத்துள் வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன்) will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky. Both let a life lived on earth earn standing in heaven, and 234 goes further by ranking it above heaven's own.

234 joins earthly renown (புகழ்) to honour in the gods' world (புத்தேள் உலகு). 966 names the same pair as the two things lost by following those who scorn you: it brings no renown and does not carry one to the gods' land (புகழ் இன்றால் புத்தேள் நாட்டு உய்யாதால்). In both verses renown here and the gods' world there are counted together, as gained in 234 and forfeited in 966.

235, as Parimelazhagar reads it, speaks of a loss that is growth for the body of renown and a death in which that body comes to exist (நத்தம் போல் கேடும் உளதாகும் சாக்காடும்). 220 says that if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin (கேடு) is worth buying even by selling oneself. Both hold that there is a கேடு worth choosing.

235 calls rare a death that is really a coming into existence. 780 says that if one can die so that the eyes of those who sustained one fill with tears, that death (சாக்காடு) is worth getting even by begging. The soldier's death in 780 is an instance, in the domain of war, of the death 235 says only the skilled achieve.

235 says a loss can be an increase. 117 says the world will not set down as ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம்) the low state of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. Both deny that the decline of a good person's fortunes is a real loss, 235 from the side of renown and 117 from the world's judgement.

236 says: if you appear, appear with renown, and for those without it not appearing is better than appearing (தோன்றலின் தோன்றாமை நன்று). 1003 says the appearance (தோற்றம்) of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown (இசை வேண்டா) is a burden to the land. Both judge a person's coming into the world by renown, and 1003 names the misers as a case of those who 'appear' without it.

Parimelazhagar reads 236 as: if born human, be born with the qualities that lead to renown. 972 says birth is alike for all living beings (பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும்) and distinction differs through the difference in what they do. On the birth reading, 972 limits 236: no one is born with renown, so the 'appearing with renown' has to be made by deeds.

On Parimelazhagar's reading of தோன்றுதல் as birth, 236 treats being born with renown as good and not being born as only the better alternative for those without it. 362 says that if one wants anything it should be not to be born (வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை), with no exception. The conflict depends on the birth reading; on Kalaignar's reading, where 236 is about entering a field of activity, the two do not meet.

237 asks why those who cannot live with renown resent the people who scorn them (இகழ்வாரை) and not themselves. 59 says those whose home does not seek renown (புகழ்புரிந்த இல் இலோர்க்கு) cannot walk with a bull's proud gait before those who scorn them (இகழ்வார் முன்). Both pair lack of renown with scorners, and both place the cause with the one scorned.

237 tells those without renown to blame themselves and not their scorners. 1060 tells the asker not to be angry at a refusal, since the affliction of his own want is witness enough (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி). In both the grievance against another person is turned back to one's own condition.

238 calls renown an எச்சம், a thing left behind, and says it is a disgrace not to obtain it (இசை என்னும் எச்சம் பெறாஅவிடின்). 114 says whether people are worthy or unworthy is seen by their எச்சம் (அவரவர் எச்சத்தாற் காணப்படும்), which Pope and Parimelazhagar take as offspring. The shared word shows 238 treating renown as a kind of offspring, the thing by which a person is judged afterwards.

238 says it is a disgrace to leave no legacy of renown. 1004 asks what the man whom no one wants (நச்சப்படாதவன்) supposes will remain as his எச்சம்; Parimelazhagar explains that he is unwanted because he has never given. 1004 applies 238's standard to the miser and finds nothing left.

239 says land that has borne a body without renown (இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்) will decline in its yield. 1003 says the appearance of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown is a burden to the land (நிலக்குப் பொறை). Both make the person without renown a weight the earth carries; 239 adds the cost to the earth.

239 says the land's rich yield shrinks (வண்பயன் குன்றும்) under a person without renown. 560 says the yield of cows shrinks (ஆபயன் குன்றும்) if the guardian does not guard. The same phrase ties natural yield to human conduct, a private person's in 239 and the king's in 560.

In 239 the land bears (பொறுத்த) a body without renown and yields less. 189 asks whether it is out of regard for virtue that the earth carries the weight (பொறை) of one who speaks ill of a person behind his back. Both picture the earth as bearing a moral load, and they differ in that 189's earth endures while 239's earth declines.

240 says those who live without blame are the ones who live, and those who live without renown are the ones who do not (வாழாதவர்). 214 says one who knows what is fitting truly lives (உயிர்வாழ்வான்) and anyone else is placed among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both redefine being alive by a moral test, and the tests are neighbours: ஒப்புரவு in 214 and the renown it earns in 240.

240 uses the formula வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் for those who live without blame. 1033 uses the same formula for those who live by eating what they plough (உழுதுண்டு வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார்), with all others following and bowing for their food. The phrase 'they alone live' is awarded on two different grounds, a good name in 240 and self-reliance in 1033.

240 says that to live without renown is not to live. 970 says the world worships and praises the radiance of those with honour who will not live when disgrace comes (இளிவரின் வாழாத மானம் உடையார்). 970 shows a person acting on 240's equation, and the result is the renown 240 demands.
